row: | | Graves, *Generating Sequences With Recurrent Neural Networks* (2013 ⚑): a soft attention window, a mixture of 10 Gaussians over the character string whose location can only move forward, lets a 3-layer, 400-cell LSTM write handwriting for given text on IAM-OnDB; the same paper's character-level LSTM reaches 1.33 bits/char (dynamic evaluation) on Hutter Prize Wikipedia | [1308.0850](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.0850) | ✓ [graves-2013-generating-sequences-recurrent-neural-networks.pdf](sources/graves-2013-generating-sequences-recurrent-neural-networks.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#attention) |

edits.old: Both papers point to Graves's handwriting model as the first differentiable attention: a soft window, a mixture of Gaussians that moves forward along the text as the pen writes
edits.new: Both papers point back to Graves's handwriting model, which Sutskever et al. credit with introducing differentiable attention: a soft window, a mixture of Gaussians that moves forward along the text as the pen writes. Bahdanau et al. name that forward-only movement as the limit their model removes, since translation needs reordering
edits.why: Only Sutskever et al. (sec. 2, p.2) call Graves's window a 'novel differentiable attention mechanism'; Bahdanau et al. (sec. 6.1) cite it as 'a similar approach of aligning' whose one-directional modes are a 'severe limitation' for MT. Neither paper calls it the first. Graves eq. 51: kappa_t = kappa_{t-1} + exp(.) confirms forward-only.

row: | | Bahdanau et al., *Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate* (ICLR 2015): a decoder that takes a softmax-weighted sum over all encoder states (additive scoring) reached 26.75 BLEU on WMT'14 En→Fr against 17.82 for a same-size fixed-vector RNN encoder–decoder, with no drop on sentences of 50+ words; it still trailed Moses (33.30) on the full test set, matching it only on sentences with no unknown words | [1409.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) | ✓ [bahdanau-2014-neural-machine-translation-jointly-learning.pdf](sources/bahdanau-2014-neural-machine-translation-jointly-learning.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#attention) |
doubts: Note's 'single model still trailed 33.30' is right for the full test set (Table 1: 26.75; the longer-trained RNNsearch-50* got 28.45), but on no-UNK sentences RNNsearch-50* scored 36.15 vs Moses 35.63. Not wrong, just one-sided; left as is.

row: | | Sutskever et al., *Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks* (NIPS 2014): a 4-layer LSTM encodes the source into one fixed vector and another decodes from it; on WMT'14 En→Fr an ensemble of 5 reached 34.81 BLEU against 33.30 for a phrase-based baseline (still below the best WMT'14 system's 37.0), and reversing the source words raised a single model from 25.9 to 30.6 BLEU | [1409.3215](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) | ✓ [sutskever-2014-sequence-sequence-learning-neural-networks.pdf](sources/sutskever-2014-sequence-sequence-learning-neural-networks.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#attention) |
doubts: 25.9->30.6 is from sec. 3.3 text; Table 1 gives single forward 26.17 vs single reversed 30.59 (beam 12). Note's figures match the text.

row: | | He et al., *Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition* (CVPR 2016): adding a parameter-free identity shortcut (`y = F(x) + x`) around every two layers fixed the degradation where a 34-layer plain net trained worse than an 18-layer one despite batch norm; on ImageNet the 34-layer ResNet reached 25.03% top-1 validation error (10-crop) against 28.54% for the plain net, and on CIFAR-10 deeper ResNets had smaller residual responses | [1512.03385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) | ✓ [he-2016-deep-residual-learning-image-recognition.pdf](sources/he-2016-deep-residual-learning-image-recognition.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#the-transformer-block-and-the-gpt-stack) |

headings.heading: The transformer block and the GPT stack

edits.old: The deeper the ResNet, the smaller its residual outputs, so each layer adjusts the signal rather than rewriting it
edits.new: On CIFAR-10, the deeper the ResNet, the smaller its residual outputs, so each layer adjusts the signal rather than rewriting it
edits.why: The layer-response analysis (sec. 4.2, Fig. 7) is on CIFAR-10 ResNet-20/56/110, not ImageNet; as written it reads as following from the preceding ImageNet sentence. Other numbers (25.03 vs 28.54, Table 2, 10-crop; 'unlikely' vanishing gradients with BN, sec. 4.1) check out.

row: | | van den Oord et al., *Pixel Recurrent Neural Networks* (ICML 2016): an image as a product of next-pixel 256-way softmaxes in raster order; the Diagonal BiLSTM reached 3.00 bits/dim on CIFAR-10 and the masked-convolution PixelCNN 3.14, with PixelCNN's parallelism limited to training since 'the image generation process is sequential for both' | [1601.06759](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06759) | ✓ [oord-2016-pixel-recurrent-neural-networks.pdf](sources/oord-2016-pixel-recurrent-neural-networks.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#prefill-decode-and-the-kv-cache) |

row: | | van den Oord et al., *Conditional Image Generation with PixelCNN Decoders* (NIPS 2016): gated, two-stack PixelCNN matched PixelRNN on CIFAR-10 (3.03 vs 3.00 bits/dim) and beat it on ImageNet 32/64, reaching PixelRNN's quality in under half the training time (60 h on 32 GPUs); sampling stays sequential, each pixel fed back into the network | [1606.05328](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05328) | ✓ [oord-2016-conditional-image-generation-pixelcnn-decoders.pdf](sources/oord-2016-conditional-image-generation-pixelcnn-decoders.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#prefill-decode-and-the-kv-cache) |

row: | | Hendrycks & Gimpel, *Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)* (2016 ⚑): GELU = xΦ(x), the expectation of a mask that zeroes inputs with probability 1−Φ(x); it beat ReLU and ELU on small benchmarks only (e.g. 7.89% vs 8.16% and 8.41% error on CIFAR-10 with a 9-layer CNN, median of 3 runs), and the paper's SiLU xσ(x), later renamed Swish, did worse than GELU | [1606.08415](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08415) | ✓ [hendrycks-2016-bridging-nonlinearities-stochastic-regularizers-gaussian.pdf](sources/hendrycks-2016-bridging-nonlinearities-stochastic-regularizers-gaussian.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#the-transformer-block-and-the-gpt-stack) |

| | Peters et al., *Semi-supervised Sequence Tagging with Bidirectional Language Models* (ACL 2017): TagLM concatenates top-layer forward and backward LM states (trained on the 1B Word Benchmark) into a tagger, raising CoNLL-2003 NER F1 from 90.87 to 91.93; an LM trained only on the CoNLL data gave no gain (90.79) | [1705.00108](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.00108) | ✓ [peters-2017-semi-supervised-sequence-tagging-bidirectional.pdf](sources/peters-2017-semi-supervised-sequence-tagging-bidirectional.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#embeddings-and-position) |
doubts: Note says 'frozen language model'. The paper says 'the LM weights are fixed' only for one ablation (p.5) and otherwise just pre-trains the LMs separately and removes the softmax; it never says outright that the main system keeps them fixed. Probably right (ELMo describes it the same way), so left unchanged.

row: | | Liu et al., *Generating Wikipedia by Summarizing Long Sequences* (ICLR 2018): a decoder-only transformer over [input; separator; output] almost halves parameters; on WikiSum the encoder–decoder could not learn at 2,000 input tokens, the decoder kept improving to 4,000 (16 GB P100 limit), and local + memory-compressed attention reached 11,000, with test log-perplexity 2.47 → 2.22 → 2.05; ROUGE-L did not follow at 4,000 (33.6 vs 34.2) | [1801.10198](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.10198) | ✓ [liu-2018-generating-wikipedia-summarizing-long-sequences.pdf](sources/liu-2018-generating-wikipedia-summarizing-long-sequences.pdf) | [01](notes/01-how-llms-work.md#prefill-decode-and-the-kv-cache) |
